The speaker moved an amendment to reject the Treasury Laws Amendment (Recovering Unpaid Superannuation) Bill 2019, arguing it provides an amnesty for employers who have not paid superannuation for 26 years and that the government is not doing enough to combat theft of workers' entitlements. The amendment calls on the government to help unions protect workers from superannuation theft and to end policy uncertainty by committing to legislated increases to the superannuation guarantee.

The speaker argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Recovering Unpaid Superannuation) Bill 2019 provides a business amnesty for unpaid superannuation, improves system integrity through expanded Single Touch Payroll, and is backed by $133.7 million for ATO compliance. He contrasted this approach with the opposition's focus on grandstanding rather than practical solutions.

The speaker supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Recovering Unpaid Superannuation) Bill 2019 as a small step, but noted only $230 million of the estimated $6 billion in unpaid super would be recovered, warned of moral hazard, and called for a 10-year moratorium on future amnesties, better ATO funding, and listing superannuation under the National Employment Standards.

The speaker argued that the ATO’s Single Touch Payroll will identify unpaid superannuation more quickly, and dismissed industry super’s multibillion-dollar figure as unverified. They also noted that the member for Whitlam declined to provide the source of his research and numbers.

The Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Income Management to Cashless Debit Card Transition) Bill 2019 transitions approximately 23,000 welfare recipients in the Northern Territory and Cape York from the BasicsCard to the cashless debit card, with the transition occurring community-by-community over nine months from 1 April 2020 and backed by almost $18 million in support. The bill also extends the cashless debit card across all four current trial sites until 30 June 2021, arguing the card provides greater consumer choice, reduces social harm, and has shown positive results such as decreases in drug and alcohol issues and crime.

The speaker opposed the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Income Management to Cashless Debit Card Transition) Bill 2019, arguing it is discriminatory, lacks evidence of effectiveness, and would not create jobs, while announcing Labor would seek to amend the bill in the Senate to make the cashless debit card voluntary in the Northern Territory unless a community requests it or individual circumstances apply.

The government is continuing the rollout of the cashless debit card, citing reduced violence, drug and alcohol issues, and improved child health and financial management, and supports the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Income Management to Cashless Debit Card Transition) Bill 2019 as part of the solution.

The speaker opposed the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Income Management to Cashless Debit Card Transition) Bill 2019, arguing it is discriminatory, lacks evidence, and would disproportionately affect First Nations Australians (80% of those on income management in the Northern Territory). The speaker called for the cashless debit card to be voluntary, supported by community consultation and wraparound services, and cited research showing a 100-gram drop in birth weights among affected populations.

The speaker opposed the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Income Management to Cashless Debit Card Transition) Bill 2019, arguing it is discriminatory and disproportionately impacts Indigenous Australians. They noted over 80% of the 23,000 people on income management in the Northern Territory are Indigenous, cited no evidence the cashless debit card works, and highlighted that communities like Milingimbi were not consulted.

The opposition opposed the bill to transition income management to a cashless debit card, arguing it is a failed, short-term solution that is discriminatory against Indigenous Australians and lacks evidence of effectiveness. They highlighted that 80% of Northern Territory recipients are Indigenous, cited research showing no improvement in child health outcomes, and called for voluntary, community-consulted programs with wraparound support instead.

The speaker opposed the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Income Management to Cashless Debit Card Transition) Bill 2019, arguing the cashless debit card expansion unfairly punishes community members who do not drink, smoke, gamble or use drugs.

The speaker argued that cashless debit card trial results are mixed and lack conclusive academic evidence, and called for delaying the bill until the University of Adelaide report is released and genuine consultation is conducted with affected remote Aboriginal communities, particularly in the Northern Territory.

The government argued the bill extends the cashless debit card trial to 30 June 2021, transitions income management participants in the Northern Territory and Cape York to the card, and limits the ministerial power to vary the restriction rate to a maximum of 80%, while removing compulsory participation for age pensioners except in Cape York.

The speaker opposed the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Income Management to Cashless Debit Card Transition) Bill 2019 and its amendments, arguing the government imposed the policy without consulting Aboriginal people in the Northern Territory. They stated the BasicsCard was already harmful, cited effective alcohol measures like floor pricing and police enforcement as alternatives, and called the blanket approach disrespectful and undemocratic.

The member argued for the Drug Testing Trial Bill, stating jobseekers testing positive would not lose welfare payments but be placed on income management for 24 months with 80% of payments quarantined. The trial will run in Canterbury Bankstown, Mandurah, and Logan, with $10 million in additional treatment funding.

The speaker opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2019, arguing it lacks evidence, contradicts expert advice, and would waste scarce counselling resources on unwilling participants while 200,000–500,000 Australians annually cannot access addiction services.

The member opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2019, arguing it is uncosted—with gold-standard tests estimated at $550–$950 each—and would not create jobs for 1.9 million Australians. They cited existing program costs and low efficacy (jobactive $1.5bn/year, Work for the Dole $1.7bn/year, PaTH $840m/year), criticised welfare churn, and referenced St Vincent de Paul data showing repeated electricity disconnections in Werribee and Hoppers Crossing.

The member for Canning argued in support of the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2019, which will trial drug testing of welfare recipients in Mandurah (WA), Logan (Qld) and Canterbury-Bankstown (NSW), claiming the measure is not punitive but aims to help those with drug and alcohol addiction into employment, with 80% of payments quarantined after a first positive test and a $10 million treatment fund available for second-time positive testees.

Labor opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2019, which would subject 5,000 Newstart and youth allowance recipients in Canterbury-Bankstown, Mandurah and Logan to random drug tests for two years. The opposition argued the measure lacks evidence, citing a New Zealand trial with less than one per cent positive results, punishes without addressing addiction, and urged instead raising the Newstart rate to stimulate the economy, citing support from the Business Council and the RBA.

The speaker argued the Drug Testing Trial Bill 2019 is a misguided attack on unemployed people, noting that expert submissions overwhelmingly opposed it while 200,000–500,000 Australians cannot access addiction services due to underfunding and 700,000 people are unemployed with 19 applicants per job. The trial would waste money on drug-testing 5,000 recipients in three locations, potentially pushing unprepared people into treatment and displacing those who genuinely seek help.

Labor opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2019, arguing it lacks a mandate and evidence, would indiscriminately drug test 5,000 welfare recipients in three areas, and cited that 98% of submissions opposed the bill and only 22 of 8,000 tested positive in a similar New Zealand trial.

The speaker opposed the Drug Testing Trial Bill, arguing it ignores expert evidence from the Royal Australasian College of Physicians that drug testing welfare recipients is harmful and ineffective, and instead called for raising welfare payments like Newstart ($279 per week) and improving Centrelink services.

Centre Alliance opposed the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2019 for the third time, arguing it lacks published costings, citing US programs that cost around $2,650 per positive test and were largely ineffective, and calling the bill a distraction from the need to raise Newstart and address harms from robo-debts.

The Social Services Legislation Amendment (Drug Testing Trial) Bill 2019 introduces a two‑year trial of random drug testing for 5,000 new Newstart and youth allowance recipients in Canterbury Bankstown, Logan, and Mandurah, with positive results leading to income management and, after a second positive test, compulsory treatment supported by an additional $10 million treatment fund.

The speaker opposed the National Disability Insurance Scheme Amendment (Streamlined Governance) Bill 2019, arguing it would lower the standard for appointing NDIA board members from requiring all states and territories' support to a simple majority. They cited a University of Western Australia report highlighting the NDIS's $4 billion+ underutilisation, unsustainability, and major gaps in responsibility and funding between governments.

The speaker supported the NDIS Amendment (Streamlined Governance) Bill 2019 to reduce delays in board appointments, criticised the withholding of draft plans from participants, and urged the government to address the exclusion of people who acquire a disability after age 65 from accessing the NDIS.

The National Disability Insurance Scheme Amendment (Streamlined Governance) Bill 2019 simplifies rule-making and decision-making under the NDIS Act and ensures the Royal Commission into Violence, Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation of People with Disability has clear authority to obtain information from the NDIA and NDIS Commission.

This bill would tighten rules on unions and employer groups after a royal commission found misconduct.
It would let the Federal Court ban officials from office and cancel an organisation's registration for serious breaches.
New rules would also block a merger that is not in the public interest.
Include serious criminal offences as a ground for automatic disqualification from office.
Empower the Federal Court to disqualify officials who repeatedly break industrial laws or are not fit and proper.
Create an offence for a disqualified person to still act as an official.
Allow the Federal Court to cancel registration for unlawful conduct or serious criminal offences.
Expand the Federal Court's power to appoint an administrator to fix governance problems.
Introduce a public interest test for amalgamations, considering each organisation's compliance record among other things.
Registered employee and employer organisations and their officials.

The speaker moved to reject the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019, arguing it attacks unions instead of addressing wage theft, stagnant wages (growing eight times slower than profits), and over 200 workplace deaths per year, and that its provisions—allowing any person of sufficient interest to disqualify officials or deregister unions—would be weaponised by employers like Liberal donor Gerry Hanssen.

The speaker argued in support of the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019, which would expand grounds for disqualifying union officials and make it a criminal offence for disqualified persons to hold office. The speaker cited the CFMMEU as having been fined over $16 million, with over 2,000 breaches and 74 representatives before the courts, and described alleged union intimidation and thuggery, including the physical assault of a volunteer.

The speaker argued that the government is not anti-union but opposes unions that break the law, specifically targeting the CFMMEU for over 2,000 incidents of law-breaking and $16 million in fines. He supported the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019, which would make it easier for the Federal Court to deregister organisations like the CFMMEU and disqualify officials convicted of serious offences or repeated industrial law breaches.

The speaker argued that the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019 is an attack on unions and workers, violating human rights and international law, and would further suppress wages—citing a 50‑year low in workers’ share of income, penalty rate cuts costing some workers up to $26,000, and total losses of $2.9 billion.

The speaker opposed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019, arguing it is an obsessive government attack on unions that would suppress wages, violate international labour rights, and undermine democratic representation. They noted the bill goes beyond the Heydon royal commission recommendations, is largely unchanged from a 2017 version, and contrasts with the government's failure to establish a national anticorruption commission.

The speaker argued the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019 is needed to tackle illegal behaviour by unions and employer organisations, citing CFMMEU official John Setka’s 59 convictions and union intimidation during the Boothby election campaign. The bill would give courts greater powers to disqualify officials, cancel registrations, and enforce accountability for law-breaking organisations.

The speaker opposed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment (Ensuring Integrity) Bill 2019, arguing it allows employers or others to deregister unions and disqualify officials via a fit-and-proper-person test.
